 Walt Rothwell: This year's COLA helps, but Social Security still at risk
 The fund remains a vital lifeline for retirees, people with disabilities and their survivors. Now, more than ever, it needs the support of public officials to preserve it. 
 Walt Rothwell Contributed 
 By 
 Walt Rothwell 
 Today at 8:00 AM 
 Listen
 Comments
 Share
 Share this article 
 Opinion
 Opinion 
 Advocates for ideas and draws conclusions based on the interpretation of facts and data. 
 The Trust Project
 What is this? 
 For one in five Minnesotans, the annual Social Security cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is more than a number. It helps to cover the costs of everyday essentials which are stretching the household budgets of all Minnesotans. Grocery, fuel, and healthcare bills are all at issue, not to mention cuts in other “safety net” services.
 A 3.6% increase announced recently is vitally important to Americans who rely on Social Security to make ends meet, including retirees, people with disabilities, and their survivors. The automatic annual COLA was mandated in the 1970s, thanks to the voices of AARP and other retiree organizations, to protect the vulnerable from ever-rising prices. Before then, an act of Congress was required for any step to help cope with inflation, and these came ad hoc at irregular intervals.
 ADVERTISEMENT 
 While the Social Security COLA helps, it is always “chasing” these rising costs. For those with a fixed income, even modest cost increases force difficult choices among basic needs.
 My wife’s brother became eligible for Social Security disability benefits in 2006, at age 56, following a brain injury. We brought him to Rochester to support him until his death in 2024. The Social Security compensation allowed him to live independently for several years until dementia progressed and he required memory care. Social Security also protected the financial security of his aging parents, who relied on their own retirement benefits during those difficult years.
 Social Security is central to the financial security of older Americans, people with disabilities, and their survivors. Workers pay into the fund with every paycheck, and by retirement have earned their benefit over decades. Social Security belongs to them, and they must be able to “bank” on it.
 A recent AARP survey makes clear just how much is at stake with our federal policy. Half of Social Security recipients report this as their primary source of income. Even with a modest annual upward adjustment, too many older Americans still find themselves falling behind.
 Special interests in Washington continue to push ideas that would erode the COLA or current benefit levels. Such proposals are out of touch with the reality facing vulnerable Americans across our state.
 This year's COLA matters; each additional dollar counts when families are paying more for groceries, health care, and other necessities. AARP is a central voice fighting to protect and strengthen Social Security into the future. Congress must take action to ensure Social Security is solvent for the generations still paying into the fund each payday, without cutting the benefit they have earned.
 Now, with the election over and candidates prepare to begin their fresh terms in office, please express your concerns and ask questions — especially of your federal officeholders. The message from Minnesotans must be clear: Keep the promise. Protect and strengthen Social Security for decades to come for the Americans who continue to earn it.
 ADVERTISEMENT 
 Walt Rothwell is a retired healthcare worker and community volunteer who lives in Rochester.
